evidence.claim: The numbered road first connected Lebanon center and Baltic as part of Highway 354, designated in 1922.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the road from Taftville via Baltic and North Franklin to Lebanon center, was designated as a secondary state highway known as Highway 354.

evidence.claim: That section became Route 207 in 1932. Westward extensions reached Exeter in 1935 and Hebron in 1940.
evidence.quote: The portion of old Highway 354 between Lebanon center and Baltic was renumbered to Route 207 in the 1932 state highway renumbering.

evidence.claim: That section became Route 207 in 1932. Westward extensions reached Exeter in 1935 and Hebron in 1940.
evidence.quote: In 1935, Route 207 was extended west to the village of Exeter (at Route 16), and further westward to Hebron center (at Route 85) in 1940.

evidence.claim: Later changes addressed the drive itself: a Franklin section was rebuilt to improve its grade in 1961, and the eastern terminus moved to its present location in 1962.
evidence.quote: The eastern terminus was moved to its current location in 1962. In 1961, a section in Franklin was reconstructed and realigned to improve the grade.

evidence.claim: Those highway changes linked places with older histories. At Lebanon, the War Office and Jonathan Trumbull’s home had directed Connecticut’s Revolutionary War effort; farther east, Baltic developed beside a cotton mill on the Shetucket.
evidence.quote: Connecticut's effort during the Revolutionary War was directed from the War Office on the Green and the adjacent home of Governor Jonathan Trumbull Sr.

evidence.claim: Hebron’s old green survives in pieces on either side of Main Street, divided by twentieth-century highway widening and realignment.
evidence.quote: The town green now survives only in fragmented portions on either side of Main Street (Route 66), owing to 20th-century highway widening and alignment.

evidence.claim: At the junction of Routes 66 and 85, the village center has served the town’s civic life since incorporation in 1708.
evidence.quote: Centered on the junction of Connecticut Routes 66 and 85, it has served as the rural community's civic center since its incorporation in 1708.

evidence.claim: The green once held a colonial meetinghouse; a tavern, shop and gristmill followed.
evidence.quote: Its town green, also the site of a colonial meeting house, was the only civic focal point of consequence in its early years, later augmented by a tavern, shop, and gristmill.

evidence.claim: Nineteenth-century fires destroyed virtually all the village’s eighteenth-century buildings. Only a handful of early nineteenth-century houses survive.
evidence.quote: A series of fires in the 19th century wiped out virtually all of the village's 18th-century buildings, and only a handful of early 19th-century houses survive.

evidence.claim: The historic district also includes churches and the Douglas Library, while war memorials occupy the surviving portions of the green. Highway changes have altered the common’s shape.
evidence.quote: Also included are 19 non-contributing buildings and six war memorials (non-contributing objects) on the surviving elements of the Hebron Green. In addition to many 19th-century houses, several churches and the town public library (Douglas Library) are also included in the district.

evidence.claim: Baltic grew around a cotton mill on the Shetucket River, on land purchased by William Sprague III in 1856.
evidence.quote: Baltic was formed around a cotton mill established on the Shetucket River on land purchased in 1856 by former Rhode Island Governor and Senator William Sprague III.

evidence.claim: After the first mill burned, Frederick Sayles bought the site and built a replacement that opened in 1899.
evidence.quote: Frederick Sayles of Pawtucket, Rhode Island purchased the site. He built the Baltic Mills Co. cotton mill which opened in 1899.

evidence.claim: Manufacturing continued until 1967; the property later served a mail-order operation.
evidence.quote: The mill continued operating until 1967, when it was closed and the property and equipment were sold. In 1970, the property was sold to the Casper Division of Bevis Industries, which used it for a mail order operation.

evidence.claim: Fire destroyed the mill’s remains in 1999, leaving one critically damaged building.
evidence.quote: In August 1999, the remains of the mill were destroyed by fire. There was only one building that survived, although it was also critically damaged.

evidence.claim: The historic district encompasses virtually the entire village, extending the story beyond the factory site.
evidence.quote: encompassing virtually the entire extent of the village.

evidence.claim: Listed on the National Register in 1987, the district includes 210 contributing structures across 122 acres, preserving the scale of the mill village.
evidence.quote: The historic district includes 210 contributing structures over a 122-acre (49 ha) area.

flags: The state data confirms designation but supplies no scenic-value narrative. Cache driving description is limited to ponds, settlements, turns and a historical grade improvement; no road width or journey time added.

War Office dates conflict: 1730 in the district article versus about 1732 in its own article. Council totals and meeting locations also conflict with Lebanon’s account. Dropped the current 1730 date and the over-1,100 meetings mostly at home claim pending stronger evidence.
Baltic’s first mill fire is dated 1887 in the village article and 1877 in Sprague’s article. Date omitted; replacement distinguished from original.
Hebron Center is an excursion at the western end, not on Route 207 itself. No current site-opening claims made.
Preserved story motifs: Hebron’s historical gristmill supports gristmill. Baltic’s retained gristmill moment motif is an inherited mismatch with its cotton-mill subject.
